title: Who is worthier than you
hook: tradition says the nine-year-old told his father no one was worthier to answer the Kashmiris' plea
tomorrow: a court of poets at Anandpur

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child at Patna: armies of children, archery by the Ganges, chickpeas in Rani Maini's lap. Your line was the boy by the river. Did you do one thing just for fun? Day eighty-two.

Sometimes a child says the thing the adults have been circling for hours. The family is arguing about whether to move grandma in, and a seven-year-old says, well, she's lonely, isn't she? The room goes quiet. Everyone knew. Nobody had said it. Go back to day seventy-seven: Anandpur, 1675. The pandits of Kashmir have told their story. The Guru is sitting in silence, heavy with it. The boy from Patna is about nine now, living with his father at last. He walks in, sees his father's face, and asks what's wrong. Today, what the nine-year-old said.
screen: `A CHILD SAYS WHAT EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `BACK TO ANANDPUR, 1675.` → `WHAT'S WRONG, FATHER?`

segments.voice: Here is the exchange as Sikh tradition tells it. The boy asks his father why he is so quiet. Guru Tegh Bahadur explains, simply, what the pandits have come for: they're being forced to give up their faith, and nobody can protect them. And then he says the hard part out loud. It would take the sacrifice of a great and holy person to stop this. The boy thinks about it, the way children do, completely seriously. And he answers: who could be worthier than you, father? That's the whole story. A handful of words from a nine-year-old. Tradition is clear that the boy understood what he was saying. He was offering his father. And his father heard it not as a child's mistake, but as an answer. Tradition says the Guru was glad, because he saw that his son was ready to lead. He told the pandits to go to the authorities and say: if Guru Tegh Bahadur accepts conversion, we all will. Then he named Gobind Rai as the next Guru, and set out for Delhi, knowing where the road went. You already know the rest. What Sikhs take from this moment is the courage of the boy. A child of nine gave up his father for people who weren't even his community, because it was right. That boy became the tenth Guru. The line people carry from it is simpler: when something needs doing, and you're wondering who should do it, sometimes the honest answer is: who better than you?

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone who faces something hard. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone standing at the edge of something difficult: a surgery, a hard conversation, a new job, a decision they're afraid of. Picture their face. Then picture yourself saying to them, simply and warmly: you can do this. Who better than you? Notice how it feels to believe in someone out loud. Let that settle in. The bell holds the time.
Who is worthier than you. Tradition says the nine-year-old Gobind Rai said it to his father, who then went to Delhi for the pandits of Kashmir.
screen: `WHO IS WORTHIER THAN YOU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: who better than you. Today, send the person you thought of a message of real encouragement. Day eighty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs often tell this story to children, and honor Guru Gobind Singh as the one who, at nine, encouraged his father to stand for the Kashmiri pandits.

fork.setup: you're nine. your father says it would take a great and holy person's sacrifice to save the pandits. what do you say?
options: who could be worthier than you?
fork.reveal: tradition says Gobind Rai answered: who could be worthier than you? his father heard it as the answer, and named him Guru.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Gobind Rai, the tenth Guru's name before he became Gobind Singh.

trapdoor: what you thought: a child said something sweet.
what it means: a nine-year-old saw what was right and offered his own father for people of another faith.
what a scholar hears: the exchange comes from later Sikh tradition; historians date the Guru's departure for Delhi to 1675, the year of his death.
